sense: a train’s puffing, in children’s talk

evidence: Verg. A. 8.421 (Lewis & Short s.v. anhēlō): fornācibus ignis anhēlat
terms.comment: We have found no word for the sound in Traupman or Morgan–Owens, and trains are modern. The classical verb for panting, which Vergil uses of the fire in the Cyclopes’ furnaces, applied by us to the puffs of a steam engine.

terms.gloss: whistle, hiss (of the train’s whistle and steam)
evidence: Ov. Met. 12.279 (Lewis & Short s.v. sībilō): of red-hot iron hissing in water
terms.comment: The classical verb for a hiss or a whistle, in its own sense: here the train’s whistle and its steam. The noun is sībilus (Traupman 45, 406).

phrases.english: Do you hear the train puffing?

sources: Lewis & Short: anhelo · Lewis & Short: sibilo
No ancient form of the sound is known; the uses are ours, on the classical verbs.
The example sentence marked “composed” is ours.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 45, 406.
